newsitem.title: ITALY: Prodi hearing in Italy resuming, no decision seen.
newsitem.headline: Prodi hearing in Italy resuming, no decision seen.

text.p: A committal hearing to decide if Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi should stand trial for alleged abuse of office and conflict of interest was due to resume on Friday after a six-week adjournment.

Sources close to the case, connected to Prodi's past chairmanship of state industrial holding IRI, said they did not expect the examining judge to reach a decision at the closed door session on whether to indict Prodi and six other people.
The hearing was due to start at 1430 GMT. Prodi was scheduled to record a television interview at the same time and will not attend.
Prodi denies the allegations, which relate to IRI's controversial sale of food group Cirio in October 1993 when he was chairman, and says he will not resign over the affair.

Prosecutor Giuseppa Geremia alleges that Prodi and five other IRI board members at the time awarded an "unjust advantage" to a little-known southern Italian consortium, Fis.Vi., in its purchase of Cirio.
The consortium's former chief executive, Carlo Saverio Lamiranda, is the seventh defendant.

Prodi's lawyer Paola Severino said presiding judge Edoardo Landi's first task on Friday would be to consider a request from one of the defendants, Mario Draghi, for a court-appointed investigation into the financial regularity of the Cirio sale.
"The judge can decide to accept it or reject it," Severino said. Acceptance would lead to a further adjournment.
Draghi, director general of the Treasury Ministry, was a member of the IRI board at the time of the 310 billion lire ($184 million) sale.
Prodi, who has headed a centre-left coalition since last May, has suffered no evident political damage from the case, which does not involve any allegations of personal enrichment.
Cirio, best known for its canned tomatoes, was sold privately to Fis.Vi after IRI decided that offers submitted in a public tender did not meet the right conditions.
Fis.Vi soon after sold the company's olive oil interests to the Anglo-Dutch group Unilever, for which Prodi had worked as a consultant, and has since divested itself of the whole group.
Prodi denies his relationship with Unilever held any conflict of interest, saying he had cut his ties months earlier, in May 1993, when he became chairman of IRI for a second time.
The hearing technically opened on January 15 but was adjourned until Friday after just 40 minutes because one of the defence lawyers was engaged on another case.
